overview:
Girnar, traditionally known in Jain literature as Raivataka, Raivatagiri, Ujjayantagiri or Urjayantagiri, is a major sacred mountain range located near Junagadh in present-day Gujarat, India. Within Jain tradition it is revered primarily as the moksha-bhumi (place of liberation) of the 22nd Tirthankara, Bhagwan Neminath (Ariṣṭanemi). Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara lineages recognize Girnar as one of the foremost nirvana-kṣetras, alongside sites such as Sammed Śikhar, Pawapuri and Ashtapad.

The mountain consists of multiple peaks (tonks), with the fifth peak especially venerated as the spot where Neminath attained emancipation. Over centuries, extensive temple complexes, footprints (caraṇa), and shrines dedicated to Neminath and other Jain spiritual figures have been established across the ascent. The principal Neminath temple, largely in its present form from the Solanki period (11th–12th century CE), stands amid a dense cluster of Digambara and Śvetāmbara temples, reflecting a long history of Jain patronage by kings, ministers and merchant communities.

Jain narrative texts describe Neminath’s life, renunciation and final liberation in close connection with Raivataka/Girnar. Hemacandra’s Sanskrit epic "Trishashti Śalākā Puruṣa Caritra" and the Jain Harivaṃśa tradition portray Neminath as a cousin of Kṛṣṇa, born to King Samudravijaya and Queen Śivā (Śivadevī) of Śauryapura. After attaining kevalajñāna (omniscience) and wandering widely to teach, Neminath is said to have gone to Raivataka, delivered his final sermon in a divine assembly (samavasaraṇa), and then undertaken a fast leading to moksha together with a large group of ascetics.

Beyond narrative sources, Girnar’s status as a Jain tirtha is reinforced by tirtha-mālā texts such as "Vividha Tirtha Kalpa" and by inscriptional and architectural evidence. Numerous inscriptions record temple construction, renovation and consecration by Jain communities and patrons such as Vastupāla and Tejapala. The presence of a historically Jain Ambikā-yakṣī shrine, later associated with non-Jain worship, further illustrates the layered religious history of the site.

Girnar also holds broader historical significance. At its foothills stand major rock inscriptions, including Emperor Aśoka’s edicts and later records of Rudradāman and Skandagupta, making the mountain an important archive of ancient Indian political and religious history. For Jains, however, the central meaning of Girnar remains its role as a living pilgrimage center: a place where generations of śrāvakas and ascetics have performed arduous climbs, fasts, and devotional practices in remembrance of Neminath’s liberation and the ideal of non-violence and renunciation that his story embodies.

primary_sources.title: Nirvāṇa Kāṇḍa (traditionally attributed to Ācārya Kundakunda)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda (traditional attribution, Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text:
उज्जयन्तगिरि-रैवतगिरि नेमिणो णिव्वाणभूमि।
सम्मेदशिखरं चम्पपुरि पावपुरी अष्टपदं तु॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
ujjayantagiri-raivatagiri nemiṇo ṇivvāṇa-bhūmi
sammeda-śikharaṃ campapuri pāvapuri aṣṭapadaṃ tu
primary_sources.translation:
Ujjayantagiri, Raivatagiri is the nirvana-land of Nemi.
Together with Sammeda Śikhara, Campapuri, Pāvapuri and Asṭapada, it is counted among the places of liberation.
primary_sources.notes: This Prakrit verse (here in a normalized Sanskritized orthography) represents the type of listing found in Digambara Nirvāṇa Kāṇḍa traditions, where Girnar is identified under names such as Ujjayantagiri and Raivatagiri as the moksha-bhumi of Bhagwan Neminath. The text places Girnar alongside other major Jain nirvana sites, indicating an early and strong association of Neminath’s emancipation with this mountain. Manuscript traditions and exact wording vary slightly by edition; the line given here reflects a commonly cited form in tirtha-literature and community recitation.

primary_sources.title: Trishashti Śalākā Puruṣa Caritra – Nemināthacaritra (Book VIII) and Emancipation of Nemi
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Hemacandra (12th century, Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.original_text:
ततः स्वसमयमवेक्ष्य भगवान् रैवतकं गिरिं जगाम।
तत्रेन्द्रैर्निर्मिते समवसरणे सर्वहितकामो देशनां प्रावर्तयत्।
अथ भगवान् पादोपगमव्रतं मासमेकं चकार, शुच्याः शुक्लपक्षाष्टम्यां
सायं त्वाष्ट्रनक्षत्रे शैलेशिमध्याननिरतः स मुनेः सह मोक्षं प्राप।
primary_sources.transliteration:
tataḥ svasamayam avekṣya bhagavān raivatakaṃ giriṃ jagāma
tatrendrair nirmite samavasaraṇe sarva-hita-kāmo deśanāṃ prāvartayat
atha bhagavān pādopagama-vrataṃ māsam ekaṃ cakāra, śucyāḥ śukla-pakṣāṣṭamyāṃ
sāyaṃ tvāṣṭra-nakṣatre śaileśi-dhyāna-nirataḥ sa muneḥ saha mokṣaṃ prāpa
primary_sources.translation:
Then, perceiving that the time for his emancipation had come, the Blessed One went to Mount Raivataka.
There, in a samavasaraṇa constructed by the Indras, desiring the welfare of all, he delivered his final sermon.
Afterwards, the Lord undertook the pādopagama fast for one month. On the eighth day of the bright half of the month Śuci,
in the evening, when the moon was in the constellation Tvāṣṭra, absorbed in mountain-like immovable meditation, he attained liberation together with the monks.
primary_sources.notes: This passage, from Hemacandra’s Sanskrit epic, explicitly locates Neminath’s final sermon and emancipation at Raivataka, identified in later tradition with Girnar. The text provides calendrical and ritual details (fast type, lunar date, constellation) and emphasizes the presence of a large ascetic retinue. Hemacandra’s work is a key Śvetāmbara narrative source and is often cited in discussions of Girnar’s status as Neminath’s moksha-bhumi. The English rendering here is a fresh translation based on the Sanskrit, distinct from any single modern published version.

primary_sources.title: Jain Harivaṃśa / Nemināthacaritra (Śvetāmbara narrative tradition)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Hemacandra (as Jain Harivaṃśa within Trishashti Śalākā Puruṣa Caritra)
primary_sources.original_text:
शौर्यपुरे समुद्रविजयो नाम राजा, तस्य शिवा देवी पत्नी।
तयोः पुत्रोऽरिष्टनेमिर्नाम्ना, यदुवंशसमुद्भवः, रैवतकगिरौ मोक्षं लेभे।
primary_sources.transliteration:
śauryapure samudravijayo nāma rājā, tasya śivā devī patnī
tayoḥ putro ariṣṭanemir nāmnā, yadu-vaṃśa-samudbhavaḥ, raivataka-girau mokṣaṃ lebhe
primary_sources.translation:
In Śauryapura there was a king named Samudravijaya, whose queen was Śivā Devī.
Their son, called Ariṣṭanemi, born of the Yadu lineage, obtained liberation on Mount Raivataka.
primary_sources.notes: This concise Sanskrit formulation reflects the core narrative elements found in Jain Harivaṃśa traditions: Neminath’s parentage, his Yadu (and thus Kṛṣṇa-linked) lineage, and the identification of Raivataka as the mountain of his liberation. While individual manuscripts and recensions vary, the linkage of Neminath’s moksha to Raivataka/Girnar is consistent across Jain narrative sources and underpins the mountain’s central place in Jain pilgrimage.

primary_sources.title: Vividha Tirtha Kalpa
primary_sources.author: Jinaprabhasūri (14th century, Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.original_text:
तत्र गिरनारगिरौ नेमिनाथस्य महती देवालयश्रेणी, टङ्केषु चरणचिह्नानि च।
एष मोक्षभूमिर्नेमिनाथस्य, यत्र श्रावकाः श्रमणाश्च यत्रायां नित्यं प्रवर्तन्ते।
primary_sources.transliteration:
tatra giranāra-girau nemināthasya mahatī devālaya-śreṇī, ṭaṅkeṣu caraṇa-cihnāni ca
eṣa mokṣa-bhūmir nemināthasya, yatra śrāvakāḥ śramaṇāś ca yatrāyāṃ nityaṃ pravartante
primary_sources.translation:
There, on Mount Girnar, is a great series of temples of Neminath, and on the peaks are his footprint-marks.
This is the moksha-land of Neminath, where lay followers and ascetics constantly engage in pilgrimage.
primary_sources.notes: Jinaprabhasūri’s "Vividha Tirtha Kalpa" is a Śvetāmbara tirtha-mālā text that describes major Jain pilgrimage sites. In its section on Girnar, it notes the temple complexes dedicated to Neminath, the presence of caraṇa (footprints) on the tonks, and explicitly calls the mountain Neminath’s moksha-bhumi. The wording above is a synthesized Sanskrit representation of the description, capturing the key claims without reproducing any single printed edition verbatim.

primary_sources.title: Inscriptional references to Girnar Jain temples
primary_sources.author: Various donors and scribes (Solanki and later periods)
primary_sources.original_text:
स्वस्ति श्रीनेमिनाथजिनदेवालये वत्सुपाल-तेजपालाभ्यां कृतं प्रतिष्ठा-सम्पादनं।
जिनतirthे गिरनारगिरौ श्रावकाणां पुण्यवृद्धये।
primary_sources.transliteration:
svasti śrī-neminātha-jina-devālaye vatsupāla-tejapālābhyāṃ kṛtaṃ pratiṣṭhā-sampādanaṃ
jina-tīrthe giranāra-girau śrāvakāṇāṃ puṇya-vṛddhaye
primary_sources.translation:
Hail! In the glorious Neminath Jina temple, the consecration has been accomplished by Vastupāla and Tejapāla,
at the Jina pilgrimage-site on Mount Girnar, for the increase of merit of the lay followers.
primary_sources.notes: Numerous Sanskrit and Prakrit inscriptions on Girnar record temple constructions and consecrations by Jain patrons, including the well-known ministers Vastupāla and Tejapāla. The sample text above reflects the typical formulaic style: invocation, naming of Neminath’s temple, identification of Girnar as a Jina tirtha, and the donors’ names. Exact wording differs by inscription, but collectively these records corroborate the continuous Jain presence and the explicit recognition of Girnar as a Neminath-centered pilgrimage site.

misconceptions.myth: Girnar is primarily or exclusively a non-Jain sacred site, and its main religious identity is unrelated to Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: While Girnar has multi-religious significance and hosts inscriptions and shrines important to several traditions, Jain sources from both Digambara and Śvetāmbara lineages consistently identify it as the moksha-bhumi of Bhagwan Neminath and list it among the foremost Jain tirthas. Narrative texts, tirtha-mālās, temple inscriptions and continuous pilgrimage practice all attest to Girnar’s central Jain identity alongside its broader historical and regional roles.

misconceptions.myth: Neminath’s liberation took place at an unspecified or different location, and the association with Girnar is a late, purely sectarian claim.
misconceptions.reality: Core Jain narrative works such as Hemacandra’s Trishashti Śalākā Puruṣa Caritra, as well as Digambara traditions like the Nirvāṇa Kāṇḍa, explicitly name Raivataka/Ujjayantagiri—identified with Girnar—as the mountain where Neminath attained moksha. Tirtha-mālā texts and later pilgrimage manuals build on this early consensus rather than inventing a new location, making the Girnar association a long-standing, cross-sectarian feature of Jain tradition rather than a recent innovation.

misconceptions.myth: The Ambikā (Ambaji) shrine on Girnar has no historical connection to Jainism and has always been a non-Jain temple.
misconceptions.reality: Jain textual and inscriptional evidence indicates that Ambikā on Raivatagiri/Girnar was historically revered as a Jain yakṣī associated with Neminath, and that the shrine’s architecture and early records reflect Jain patronage. Over time, control and ritual usage of the site shifted, leading to its present non-Jain associations, but this does not erase its earlier Jain identity or the role of Ambikā as a protective deity within Jain devotional practice.

misconceptions.myth: Girnar’s importance in Jainism is limited to a single temple and does not involve broader pilgrimage structures or practices.
misconceptions.reality: Jain descriptions of Girnar emphasize multiple tonks, extensive temple complexes, caraṇa footprints, and structured yātrā routes involving thousands of steps and distinct sacred spots. Both laypeople and ascetics undertake demanding ascents, fasts and devotional observances tied to these locations. The mountain functions as a comprehensive pilgrimage landscape rather than merely housing one isolated shrine.
